query: For high-entropy alloys intended for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion, and why? Propose a controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, predict how combined degradation and its wear and corrosion components would differ from a matched baseline, define where the prediction should hold or fail, identify supporting prior evidence, and state an observation that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys (HEAs) for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, simultaneous resistance to wear and corrosion is governed by the dynamic formation and stabilization of a self-renewing passivation/tribofilm at the surface, which repairs damage from mechanical wear and limits chemical attack.
generation.material_initial_state: An HEA (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi-based alloy with Mo addition) exhibiting a multiphase microstructure that contains elements predisposed to rapid passivation.
generation.intervention: Perform in-situ tribocorrosion tests by subjecting the alloy to controlled sliding contact in a corrosive medium (e.g., 3.5% NaCl) while measuring real-time electrochemical impedance and imaging the evolving surface.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted under variable contact pressures and sliding speeds in a corrosive environment, with comparative static corrosion tests as a baseline.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and stabilization of a dynamic, re-passivating tribofilm that forms on the surface during wear.
generation.mechanism: Mechanical wear intermittently removes the protective film, but the alloy’s elements enable rapid re-passivation, dynamically restoring the film. This balance between film removal and reformation reduces both wear-induced degradation and corrosion attack.
generation.predicted_outcome: At moderate wear conditions, the alloy is expected to exhibit a lower wear rate and reduced corrosion current compared to a baseline lacking dynamic passivation. Under excessive mechanical stress or in overly aggressive corrosive media, the tribofilm may fail to reform effectively, leading to increased degradation.
generation.baseline: A matched alloy sample subjected to static corrosion tests without sliding or an alloy formulation that does not promote effective re-passivation.
generation.boundary: The prediction is expected to hold under conditions where mechanical stress is moderate enough to allow timely tribofilm reformation. At extreme contact pressures or very high aggressivity of the corrosive medium, the re-passivation mechanism may be overwhelmed, negating the resistance effects.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative relationship between sliding parameters (speed, contact pressure) and the real-time dynamics of tribofilm stabilization remains uncertain and requires further in-situ characterization.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct in-situ tribocorrosion tests in a 3.5% NaCl solution, varying contact pressures and sliding speeds. Use simultaneous electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and in-situ surface imaging (e.g., scanning probe microscopy) to monitor tribofilm formation, correlate these observations with wear and corrosion rates, and perform baseline static corrosion tests on matched samples.
measurements: Real-time tribofilm thickness and stability via surface imaging
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy to assess passivation quality
Wear rate through material loss measurements
Corrosion current density from potentiodynamic polarization tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no clear correlation is observed between the presence/stability of a dynamically formed tribofilm and improvements in wear and corrosion resistance (i.e., similar degradation rates irrespective of tribofilm dynamics), or if the tribofilm forms without any measurable impact on performance compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

The results show that after annealing at 800 °C for 1 h, the formation of a dense ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer on the surface actively prevents the oxidation from continuing, so that the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film exhibits excellent oxidation resistance at 800 °C in air. The improved corrosion resistance is primarily attributed to the formation of a dense Al2O3 passivation layer on the FeCoNiCuAl alloy, which enhances its protective properties. Furthermore, Si plays a crucial role during the solidification and microstructural evolution of the coating. Si acts as a heterogeneous nucleant during solidification and is subsequently pushed toward the grain boundaries due to surface tension effects. These segregated Si particulates pin the grain boundaries through the zener pinning mechanism, which effectively inhibits grain boundary migration. Grain boundaries typically possess higher surface energy compared to grains and sub-grains, making them more susceptible to corrosive attack. However, the presence of Si particulates along the grain boundaries reduces the boundary energy and provides additional resistance to localized corrosion at these high-energy sites. This microstructural stabilization, combined with the formation of a dense and stable passivation film [], results in significantly improved corrosion resistance of the coatings in NS4 solution. decision.trend: Early work on refractory and multi-principal-element alloys (e.g., CrMoNbWV) focused on combining solid-solution or precipitate-hardening strategies with powder consolidation (via mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering) to enhance strength and wear resistance under corrosive conditions. Later efforts employed targeted microstructural refinement (e.g., by laser cladding AlCoCrFeNiMo-based alloys) to achieve simultaneous improvements in wear and corrosion performance by forming robust multiphase or nanostructured overlays. Most recently, adjusting phase fractions (for instance, FeCoNiCuAlSix coatings) has further revealed that the synergy between passivation film stability under mechanical stress and the dynamic formation of protective tribofilms remains a key unsolved mechanism restricting the design of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) for truly harsh corrosive mechanical environments.
decision.unsolved: A unifying model that fully explains how tribological contact, surface reactions, and passivation behavior interact to resist both wear and corrosion under simultaneous mechanical and chemical stress remains elusive. It is unclear how short-lived surface films, third-body debris, or near-surface microstructure evolution contribute to—versus undermine—the protective role of passivation in harsh conditions.
decision.lever: Perform in-situ tribocorrosion tests using a sliding contact in a controlled corrosive medium, combining real-time electrochemical impedance measurements with advanced surface imaging (e.g., in-situ scanning probe or synchrotron-based techniques) to monitor dynamic passivation film formation and tribofilm evolution at different contact pressures and sliding speeds.
decision.why: This approach directly targets the hypothesized mechanism that resistance to combined wear and corrosion is governed by how effectively the alloy’s evolving near-surface layer and re-passivating films protect against tribological damage and localized chemical attack. An in-situ setup allows correlation of mechanical wear processes with electrochemical data and direct observation of tribofilm formation or failure. A robust correlation (or lack thereof) between stable passivation/tribofilm development and reduced synergy would support (or falsify) the hypothesis that these protective films govern alloy resistance in corrosive mechanical environments.
